quoted.text:
AI demand is a barbell, with the labs on one end and enterprise cost-cutting on the other. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy says the biggest market sits in the middle, and inference is still "an order of magnitude too expensive" to reach it.

"On one end of the barbell are the AI labs who are consuming gobs and gobs of compute, unlike anything I've seen. And then a few runaway apps, ChatGPT, Claude Code, things like that."

"On the other end of the barbell are enterprises who are largely using AI for cost avoidance and productivity, so automating customer service or fraud or business process automation."

"In the middle of the barbell are the current production workloads of enterprises, many of which are using AWS and using inference today, but I would say the overwhelming majority of which still aren't in any pervasive way."

"And that I think is gonna be the largest absolute segment of AI usage."

"The cost of inference has come down quite a bit in the last few years, but it's still an order of magnitude too expensive, in my opinion, for it to be used as pervasively as possible."

"If you're asking enterprises to rewrite their applications that use CPU today with AI accelerators... the amount of incremental benefit they have to get is a much higher bar to want to rewrite those apps. But if you can take the cost of inference down, that bar is much lower, and all applications are gonna be better and smarter and more capable."

Today’s GPT-6 Cyber release is a meaningful step for defenders: stronger vulnerability research and better alignment. We’ve already been using GPT-6 Cyber alongside GPT-6 Astra with Daybreak to harden our own systems, finding weaknesses, validating their impact, and developing fixes.

Even after years @OpenAI, model capabilities continue to surprise me. One small example came from testing a prerelease version of GPT-6 Astra earlier this summer. We were examining tools used across our research infrastructure and one of our research infra leads, Michael Dalton, was looking into some low risk areas like a math task grader that used SymPy, a mathematics library, to check answers.

In an offline test, the submitted answer used characters that looked like ordinary letters to get past the grader’s checks. It caused the grader to run a shell command that printed “4242”, while still returning the expected result, 1/2. The grader marked the answer correct. A valid math answer had become a way to run code inside the grader - diagram below.

This is the kind of vulnerability that can be very hard for a human to find, even with a fuzzer. It takes connecting how input validation and evaluation interact, constructing an input that passes the checks but triggers unintended behavior, and recognizing the failure even when the final answer is correct. Models can reason across those pieces and help uncover classes of vulnerabilities that are difficult to spot when reviewing components in isolation.

That’s why it’s important for more defenders to use models with Daybreak to find and fix vulnerabilities in their own systems. Whether it’s a potentially internet-melting bug like PHP2Shell or a subtle but important issue like this grader bug, finding it before an attacker does gives defenders time to act.

Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers.

We’re also expanding Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT‑6 Astra to more organizations and individual security researchers - let us know if you’re interested:

Features:

Quick mini thread on tail risk hedging thanks to my man, @Fink_Money 

Tail hedging is a pretty complex topic and there are 10 more reasons why it can be challenging for a smaller investor to implement. But two of the biggest limitations from an infrastructure perspective is understanding what exactly to buy and how much to pay. Trying to execute on those two simple concepts have further nodes that have its own challenges. 

Ultimately, you’re trying to answer two questions. Which tails do you want to own, and at what price does owning them make economic sense?

A static hedge can struggle even if you’re right about the crash. Say you only buy one-month, deep OTM puts, and the market takes six months to grind lower, with sharp rallies along the way. You can be right about where spot ends up and still watch one set of puts after another expire worthless. That’s why I don’t put much faith in one-trick-pony hedges. You need infra to guide you on a core understanding of which tenors and strikes are likely to reprice based on positioning and how well those options carry as spot moves along the skew curve. 

Execution matters just as much. Say a tail option is quoted $0.02 bid at $0.10. It’s easy to look at the offer and think, “It’s a dime. How expensive can it be?” Suppose you pay $0.10, spot sells off, vol rises, and the option reprices to $1.00. Your position is worth 10× what you paid, a 900% gain. If you can work the order at $0.05, that same move takes you to 20× what you paid, a 1,900% gain. Getting filled at a nickel lets you own twice as many contracts. That’s where you double your convexity. You own twice the exposure going into the crash because of the infra you have to post liquidity and find a real inside market before spot or vol moved at all.

That’s the part I think is hard for a retail investor or a smaller shop to replicate. Even if you identify the right tails, you still need the infrastructure and execution logic to work orders at scale across names, tenors, and deltas, all at prices that make the hedge worth owning.
 
Start adding in how to offset the bleed in a real uncorrelated fashion along with a real alpha focused monetization framework and you have tons of other considerations to make when executing something like this.
